zone: Monte Cristo Group — Barlow Pass, the townsite, Glacier Basin and Poodle Dog Pass
_areas_note: ONE trailhead serves this whole group: Barlow Pass, at the end of the pavement on the Mountain Loop Highway. The road beyond it to Monte Cristo is gated and closed to vehicles, so every objective here begins with a four-mile walk or ride up the old road and rail grade to the townsite at about 2,800 ft. From the townsite the group splits in two: the Glacier Basin trail serves Cadet, Monte Cristo Peak, Foggy Peak and the Wilmans Peaks and Spires, while the Poodle Dog Pass trail serves Silver Lake, Twin Lakes, Columbia Peak and the Columbia Glacier side of Kyes. DEL CAMPO PEAK IS EXCLUDED and it is not a Monte Cristo objective at all. Its coordinate is correct and sits nearly seven kilometres west of the rest, above Gothic Basin; it shares only the Barlow Pass car park, leaving the Monte Cristo road after about one mile at the South Fork Sauk crossing and climbing the Weden Creek trail to Foggy Lake. Its camp is Foggy Lake in Gothic Basin, which the Mountain Loop zone file already carries, so nothing here duplicates it. Also deliberately NOT duplicated from that file: the Vesper and Sloan high camps, Bedal Campground and the Verlot corridor campgrounds, all of which serve other trailheads. KYES IS A SPLIT PEAK and is kept here with a caveat: the glaciated approach over the Columbia Glacier is staged from Twin Lakes on this side, but the same summit is very commonly reached from Virgin Lake on the Blanca Lake trail, an entirely separate road and trailhead south of the divide that this zone does not cover. The Mountain Loop file describes the townsite water as filter-or-boil; that is wrong and is corrected below, because surface water through this mineralised ground carries arsenic and other heavy metals that no filter removes.

sites.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
sites.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend
sites.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
sites.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
sites.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.

sites.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
sites.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in
sites.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
sites.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
sites.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.

sites.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
sites.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on
sites.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
sites.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
sites.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.

sites.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
sites.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes
sites.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
sites.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
sites.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.

sites.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
sites.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.
sites.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
sites.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
